title: 2.8: A 210fps Image Signal Processor for 4K Ultra HD True Video Super Resolution
problem: Conventional video super-resolution treats frames as independent images, neglecting temporal and spatial redundancies in video encoding (I/P/B frames, block prediction, residuals), resulting in inefficient computation and high energy cost.
motivation: Real-time 4K video super-resolution enables streaming and conferencing over low-bandwidth connections, democratizing video quality for resource-constrained networks.
method: Instead of treating each frame as a standalone image, this processor uses the structure built into video codecs. Modern video codecs already compute motion vectors (which direction pixels moved) and residuals (the pixel differences they don't need to store) to compress efficiently—this processor feeds those directly into its super-resolution pipeline instead of starting from scratch. It processes multiple frames together through alignment and refinement stages, reusing information across frames and using pre-computed codec data. This approach achieves 210fps performance at 4K resolution with lower energy than conventional super-resolution.
key_novelty: The key innovation is directly feeding motion vectors and residuals from the video codec into super-resolution processing, rather than re-analyzing raw pixel data independently.
contributions: Codec-aware architecture exploiting I/P/B frame structure and residual encoding
Temporal redundancy exploitation through feature reuse across frames
Spatial redundancy utilization via motion vectors and block prediction
baselines: Prior VSR processors treating frames independently
primary_theme: Codec-aware 4K video super-resolution ISP exploiting temporal/spatial redundancy
